design_detail: Mendelian randomization in one cohort, UK Biobank (371 463 unrelated participants of European genetic ancestry; recruited 2006-2010, follow-up to 2016), with conventional (observational) analyses in the same participants. Instruments: variants associated with alcohol use disorder (9) and with the AUDIT-C consumption score (13) in a published genome-wide study (Kranzler et al., 2019, ref 27), from which variants associated with smoking, body mass index, physical activity, vegetable or red meat intake, self-rated health, C-reactive protein or total cholesterol were removed: the primary AUD-Restricted score kept 5 variants and the secondary AUDIT-C-Restricted score 10. Analyses: Cox models of incident disease by drinking category against abstainers, with and without six lifestyle factors; linear two-sample Mendelian randomization (inverse-variance weighted, with weighted median, MR-Egger and MR-PRESSO); allele-score analyses within drinking categories; and nonlinear Mendelian randomization (fractional-polynomial and piecewise-linear models fitted to estimates within deciles of residual intake). Selected analyses were repeated in 30 716 participants of the Mass General Brigham Biobank. The sources of the variant-exposure and variant-outcome estimates for the two-sample analysis are in eMethods 8 (not read). Labelled prospective-cohort and appraised with ROBINS-E under the round brief's rule for Mendelian randomization in one cohort, because the protocol names no instrument for this design.
can_establish: Whether a genetic score for alcohol use disorder, which also strongly predicts weekly intake in UK Biobank, is associated with higher odds of hypertension, coronary artery disease and other cardiovascular conditions; and whether the lower cardiovascular risk of light and moderate drinkers in conventional analyses shrinks when a few lifestyle factors are taken into account.
cannot_establish: That every amount of alcohol raises cardiovascular risk: the shape at low intake comes from parametric curves fitted to stratum estimates, depends on the score shifting intake by the same amount at every level of drinking (not shown in the main text), and changed with the secondary instrument; that the score acts only through alcohol (variants for alcohol use disorder may influence other behaviours, and pleiotropy was detected for HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein A); effects outside a European-ancestry UK volunteer cohort; or absolute risks.

sample.recruitment: UK Biobank volunteers (recruitment 2006-2010); unrelated participants of European genetic ancestry (eMethods 1-4, not read). Replication in the Mass General Brigham Biobank, a US hospital-based biobank (eMethods 5, not read).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Exclusions are described in eMethods 2 (not read).
sample.demographics: Mean age 56.97 (SD 7.93); 46.41% men; mean intake 9.16 (SD 10.61) US standard drinks (14 g) per week; mean body mass index 27.41; mean systolic blood pressure 140.23 mm Hg; 43 297 (11.66%) genotyped on the UK BiLEVE array (Table 1). Light drinkers' intake was 38% beer, 29% red wine, 24% white wine or champagne and 6% spirits; heavy drinkers' 38% beer, 24% red wine, 28% white wine or champagne and 7% spirits (Results › Characteristics in the UK Biobank).
sample.attrition: Not reported in the main text.
sample.selection_effects: UK Biobank is a volunteer cohort; the paper does not discuss how taking part might relate to drinking or health. Only unrelated people of European genetic ancestry were analysed. The observational reference group, abstainers, is defined as 0 drinks/week and is not split into former and lifelong non-drinkers in the main analysis; lifelong abstainers (34 423) appear only as a negative control for pleiotropy. The allele-score analyses within drinking categories and the nonlinear analyses within strata of residual intake compare people grouped by a variable that the score itself influences.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported intake at baseline, converted to US standard drinks of 14 g (eMethods 3, not read), with categories abstainers (0 drinks/week), light (>0 to 8.4), moderate (>8.4 to 15.4), heavy (>15.4 to 24.5) and a highest category (>24.5) (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph). Genetic scores as described; each was standardized to a difference of 1 drink/day using UK Biobank estimates (Methods › Genetic Instruments for Alcohol Consumption).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: In grams (editors' conversion at 14 g per drink): light up to about 118 g/week, moderate about 118-216, heavy about 216-343, highest above 343. Mean (SD) intake 4.9 (2.7) drinks/week in light and 21 (3.8) in heavy drinkers. Instrument relevance: the AUD-Restricted score was associated with intake (β 7.0 drinks/week, as expected from its scaling to 1 drink/day; P<.001), with an F statistic of 780 (Results › Associations Between Genetic Instruments and Alcohol Intake Phenotypes). The linear Mendelian randomization odds ratios are expressed per 1-SD increase in genetically predicted consumption, an SD that the main text does not define.
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking: variants associated with smoking were removed from the scores; smoking was one of the six lifestyle covariates in the observational models; multivariable nonlinear Mendelian randomization adjusted for smoking, body mass index and depression (eFigure 14, not read). Other drugs: not reported.

comparison.controls: Observational: abstainers (0 drinks/week at baseline; current non-drinkers, not separated into former and lifelong non-drinkers in the main text). Linear Mendelian randomization: per unit of genetically predicted intake; Table 2's footnote says the disease associations were tested in current drinkers. Nonlinear Mendelian randomization: curves anchored at 0 drinks/week (OR 1). Pleiotropy check: 34 423 lifelong abstainers.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Observational models adjusted only for smoking, body mass index, red meat and vegetable intake, physical activity and self-rated health, some of which (body mass index, self-rated health) may lie on the path from drinking or reflect earlier illness; no adjustment for socioeconomic position or medical history is described. Genetic: confounding of the score is addressed by removing variants, by the abstainer test and by MR-Egger; how ancestry structure was handled (for example principal components) is not described in the main text.

outcomes.instruments: Six cardiovascular phenotypes (hypertension, coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, atrial fibrillation; definitions in eTable 2, not read) and ten continuous traits (systolic and diastolic blood pressure, LDL, HDL and total cholesterol, triglycerides, apolipoproteins A and B, γ-glutamyltransferase, C-reactive protein); 31 continuous phenotypes in eTables 7-8 (not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: Case definitions are in eTable 2 (not read). Table 1 reports prevalence, which suggests that the Mendelian randomization analyses counted cases present at any time, while the Cox models used incident disease.
outcomes.operationalization: Observational: prevalence and hazard ratios by drinking category against abstainers. Mendelian randomization: odds ratio per 1-SD increase in genetically predicted consumption (linear), per 1 drink/day of allele score (within categories), or relative to 0 drinks/week along a fitted curve (nonlinear).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni within families: P<.008 for the six diseases and P<.005 for the ten continuous traits (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; outcomes from records and measurements.

analysis.effect_sizes: [Conventional; UK Biobank; reference abstainers] J- or U-shaped prevalence and hazards for all six diseases (Figure 1, eFigures 1-2; no numbers printed in the main text). [Linear Mendelian randomization; AUD-Restricted score; OR per 1-SD increase in genetically predicted consumption] hypertension 1.28 (95% CI 1.18 to 1.39; P=1.73×10−9), coronary artery disease 1.38 (1.10 to 1.74; P=6.00×10−3), myocardial infarction 1.37 (1.05 to 1.78; P=2.00×10−2), stroke 1.26 (1.04 to 1.54; P=2.10×10−2), heart failure 1.39 (1.08 to 1.78; P=9.00×10−3), atrial fibrillation 1.24 (1.08 to 1.44; P=3.00×10−3) (Table 2). [Allele score per 1 drink/day, within categories] hypertension: light 1.3 (1.1 to 1.5), moderate 1.7 (1.3 to 2.2), highest category 2.6 (1.6 to 4.2); coronary artery disease: light 1.7 (1.2 to 2.4), moderate 1.8 (1.1 to 2.8), highest 5.7 (2.4 to 13.5). [Nonlinear Mendelian randomization] quadratic models fitted better than linear ones for hypertension and coronary artery disease (P<.001) and for systolic and diastolic blood pressure and LDL cholesterol; the curves are plotted without printed values (Figures 2-3). Replication cohort: quadratic association with diastolic blood pressure (P<.001), none with systolic.
analysis.covariates: Observational adjusted model: six lifestyle factors (covariates of the baseline model in eMethods 7, not read). Multivariable nonlinear Mendelian randomization: smoking, body mass index and depression.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is reported; the paper states that it followed the STROBE reporting guideline.
analysis.selective_reporting: Nonlinear results are shown in the main text for hypertension and coronary artery disease only, with the other diseases and all-cause mortality in eFigures 6-7. Results with the secondary score that suggested a threshold (no rise in risk until about 7 to 14 drinks/week) or slight decreases in risk at modest intake are reported in one paragraph and attributed to pleiotropy in that score, while the primary score's assumptions for nonlinear analysis are not examined in the main text. The text says that analyses of the other cardiovascular phenotypes supported the primary results, although three of them did not reach the paper's own threshold of P<.008.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors say the sex-stratified nonlinear analyses had reduced power.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Conventional analyses reproduced J-shaped associations, and light and moderate drinkers had healthier lifestyles than abstainers; adjustment for six lifestyle factors made the inverse associations of moderate intake with hypertension and coronary artery disease non-significant, while in Figure 1 the light-drinking category still appears below 1 after adjustment. Genetically predicted higher intake was associated with higher odds of hypertension and coronary artery disease, and quadratic curves fitted better than straight lines. With the secondary score, piecewise analyses suggested no rise in risk below about 7 to 14 drinks/week.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points describe a "consistently risk-increasing association between all amounts of alcohol consumption" and hypertension and coronary artery disease, and the Discussion says the results substantiate earlier claims that no amount of alcohol protects against cardiovascular disease. Gaps: (1) the conclusion about light drinking comes from fractional-polynomial curves fitted to stratum estimates and fixed at OR 1 for zero intake; stratified estimates of this kind are valid only if the score changes intake by the same amount at every level of drinking, which the main text does not test, and the secondary score gave a threshold instead; (2) the primary score is built from variants for alcohol use disorder, which the authors concede is an indirect measure of usual intake; (3) the fitted curves imply very large effects (odds ratios of roughly 4 to 5 for hypertension and roughly 9 for coronary artery disease at 21 drinks/week, read approximately from Figure 2, which prints no values), far beyond the linear estimates (1.28 and 1.38 per SD) and the observational hazard ratios near that intake in Figure 1, and the paper does not reconcile them; (4) lifestyle adjustment attenuated rather than removed the lower risk of light drinkers, and the suggestion that unmeasured factors would remove it is speculation; (5) the published correction (Error in Abstract, April 2022) reworded the first sentence of the abstract's conclusions to attribute the attenuation to adjustment for lifestyle factors, which matches the data; the PMC text still carries the original sentence.

timeline.event: Holmes et al. (European ancestry, ADH1B rs1229984): carriers of the intake-lowering allele had lower odds of coronary heart disease (OR 0.90); cited here as earlier Mendelian randomization evidence.
Millwood et al. (China Kadoorie Biobank): in men, genotype-predicted intake was associated log-linearly with stroke but not with myocardial infarction; cited here.

Mukamal, Stampfer and Rimm, critique of Mendelian randomization evidence on alcohol and cardiovascular disease, listed in the project's DOI list as answering items 13-15, which include this paper; it was published online in November 2019 (in print in February 2020), about two years before this paper (online March 2022), and so cannot address it.
Larsson et al. (European two-sample Mendelian randomization, up to 94 variants): associations with stroke and peripheral artery disease, borderline with coronary artery disease; cited here.

This study, with a replication in the Mass General Brigham Biobank inside the paper: the quadratic association with diastolic blood pressure was reproduced, systolic blood pressure was not significant, and disease outcomes were not tested.

Correction, "Error in Abstract" (JAMA Netw Open 2022;5(4):e2212024; doi 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2022.12024; read on PMC, PMC9021906): the first sentence of the abstract's Conclusions and Relevance was reworded to say that adjustment for coincident favourable lifestyle factors attenuated the observational benefits of modest intake. No number was changed; the PMC full text read for this card still shows the original sentence.

replication.where_it_stands: The linear Mendelian randomization associations agree in direction with other European-ancestry studies for coronary disease and stroke (Holmes et al., 2014; Larsson et al., 2020), but not with the null east Asian result for myocardial infarction (Millwood et al., 2019). The paper's distinctive claim, that risk rises from the very first drinks, rests on nonlinear Mendelian randomization with one score and was not robust to the choice of score; it should be presented as contested until nonlinear methods that do not need a constant genetic effect across intake levels are applied and replicated. Larsson et al. (2020) also used UK Biobank outcome data, so the two are not independent.

what_would_settle_it: Nonlinear Mendelian randomization of incident cardiovascular events using instruments for usual consumption that are shown to shift intake equally across the intake range (or methods that do not need this assumption), applied in several cohorts including ones with many lifelong abstainers, and reporting the stratum-specific estimates as well as fitted curves; agreement across instruments at 0 to 14 drinks/week would show whether light drinking carries a measurable cardiovascular risk.

domains.note: Instrument independence and exclusion restriction: variants associated with eight risk factors were removed; the scores did not appear to be associated with confounders (eTables 4-6, not read); in 34 423 lifelong abstainers the score was not associated with outcomes except HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein A, a pleiotropic signal; MR-Egger intercepts were non-significant, and weighted median and MR-PRESSO agreed. Variants for alcohol use disorder may act on other behaviours, which the authors concede could mean a shared genetic basis rather than a causal effect. Ancestry: European only; the handling of population structure is not described in the main text. The observational analysis is at high risk of confounding (six covariates; abstainers include former drinkers).

Relevance: strong (F=780). The primary score tracks susceptibility to alcohol use disorder more than usual intake; intake was self-reported once; and the scale of the linear estimates (per SD, undefined) cannot be converted into grams.

For the results that carry the paper's conclusions (the curves and the category-specific estimates), participants are compared within strata of observed or residual intake, which the score influences. Shape at low intake: this is valid only if the score shifts intake by the same amount at all levels, which is not shown, and the threshold found with the secondary score suggests it may not hold. Selection into the cohort: UK Biobank volunteers of European ancestry; Table 2's footnote restricts the disease analyses to current drinkers, which would condition on a variable influenced by genotype.
Not applicable in the usual sense: the score is fixed at conception.
Exclusions and missing intake or covariate data are not reported in the main text.
Definitions in eTable 2 (not read); prevalent and incident cases appear to be mixed in the genetic analyses; misclassification is unlikely to depend on genotype.

No registered plan; nonlinear results for two of six diseases in the main text; contrary results with the secondary score reported in one sentence each, with their figures only in the supplement, and explained after the fact as pleiotropy; phenotypes that missed the stated threshold described as supporting the main results.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The linear associations of the alcohol-use-disorder score with hypertension and coronary artery disease are reasonably well protected (strong instrument, several pleiotropy-robust methods, an abstainer negative control), with some concerns about pleiotropy of behavioural variants. The paper's distinctive conclusions, risk at all levels of intake and the shape of the curve, rest on stratified nonlinear analyses whose key assumption is not examined, whose results changed with the score used, and whose fitted curves imply implausibly large effects; for those, the risk of bias is high, and the overall judgment reflects them because they are the paper's headline. The conventional analyses are at high risk of confounding and serve only to show the attenuation of the J-shape. Design label and instrument follow the round brief's rule for Mendelian randomization (the protocol is silent). Cite this card for: attenuation of UK Biobank J-shaped associations by lifestyle adjustment, and linear genetic associations of an alcohol-use-disorder score with higher odds of hypertension and coronary artery disease. Do not cite it for: risk at specific intakes such as 7 or 14 drinks/week, the statement that any amount raises cardiovascular risk, or the size of the odds ratios read from the fitted curves.

key_findings.finding: 371 463 UK Biobank participants of European genetic ancestry (mean age 57.0, SD 7.9; 172 400 men, 46%) drank a mean of 9.2 (SD 10.6) US standard drinks (14 g) per week; 121 708 (32.76%) had hypertension, 27 667 (7.45%) coronary artery disease, 14 503 (3.90%) myocardial infarction, 8710 (2.34%) stroke, 5812 (1.56%) heart failure and 14 367 (3.87%) atrial fibrillation.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics in the UK Biobank, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Drinking categories (US standard drinks of 14 g per week): abstainers 0; light >0 to 8.4; moderate >8.4 to 15.4; heavy >15.4 to 24.5; highest >24.5. Observational hazards were estimated with abstainers as the reference, then re-estimated adjusting for smoking, body mass index, physical activity, cooked vegetable intake, red meat intake and self-rated health.

Conventional analyses reproduced J- or U-shaped associations of intake with the prevalence and hazards of all six diseases. Light and moderate drinkers reported better health, smoked less, had lower body mass index, more physical activity and more vegetable intake than abstainers. Moderate intake had significantly lower hazards of hypertension and coronary artery disease in the baseline models, and these differences lost significance once the six lifestyle factors were added.
key_findings.locator: Results › Observational Associations With Cardiovascular Diseases and Lifestyle Factors, 1st paragraph; Figure 1
key_findings.note: Figure 1 prints no values. Read approximately from the enlarged figure image: at light intake (about 5 drinks/week) the hazard ratio for hypertension is about 0.78 in the baseline model and about 0.90 adjusted, and for coronary artery disease about 0.76 and 0.85, with adjusted intervals that appear to exclude 1; at moderate intake (about 13 drinks/week) the adjusted ratios are about 1.00 and 0.96. Adjustment thus removed the moderate-intake association but only attenuated the light-intake one.

key_findings.finding: The primary AUD-Restricted score was strongly associated with intake in UK Biobank (β 7.0 standard drinks per week; P<.001; F statistic 780), was also associated with other alcohol measures, and showed no apparent association with confounders (eTables 4-6, not read).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations Between Genetic Instruments and Alcohol Intake Phenotypes

key_findings.finding: Pleiotropy checks: the score was not associated with the outcomes in 34 423 lifelong abstainers, and MR-Egger intercepts were non-significant, but among lifelong abstainers the score was associated with HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein A, which the authors call a potential pleiotropic effect. Genetically predicted intake was associated with higher γ-glutamyltransferase, systolic and diastolic blood pressure and LDL cholesterol.

Linear two-sample Mendelian randomization (inverse-variance weighted; OR per 1-SD increase in genetically predicted consumption): hypertension 1.28 (95% CI 1.18 to 1.39; P=1.73×10−9); coronary artery disease 1.38 (1.10 to 1.74; P=6.00×10−3); myocardial infarction 1.37 (1.05 to 1.78; P=2.00×10−2); stroke 1.26 (1.04 to 1.54; P=2.10×10−2); heart failure 1.39 (1.08 to 1.78; P=9.00×10−3); atrial fibrillation 1.24 (1.08 to 1.44; P=3.00×10−3). The abstract rounds the first two to 1.3 (1.2 to 1.4; P<.001) and 1.4 (1.1 to 1.8; P=.006). Weighted median, MR-Egger, MR-PRESSO and analyses excluding abstainers were in the same direction.
key_findings.note: By the paper's stated threshold for the six diseases (P<.008), myocardial infarction, stroke and heart failure are not significant. The SD is not defined in the main text.

key_findings.finding: Allele-score analyses within drinking categories (OR per 1 drink/day increase in the allele score): hypertension in light drinkers 1.3 (1.1 to 1.5; P=.003), moderate 1.7 (1.3 to 2.2; P<.001), highest category 2.6 (1.6 to 4.2); coronary artery disease in light drinkers 1.7 (1.2 to 2.4; P<.001), moderate 1.8 (1.1 to 2.8; P=.02), highest 5.7 (2.4 to 13.5). In male light drinkers, hypertension 1.4 (1.1 to 1.8; P=.01); in female light drinkers, coronary artery disease 1.7 (0.9 to 3.0), not significant.

Nonlinear Mendelian randomization with the primary score: three tests favoured nonlinear over linear models for hypertension and coronary artery disease, quadratic models fitted best (both P<.001), and every amount of intake was associated with higher risk, rising more steeply at higher intake, including between 1 and 2 drinks per day; similar quadratic shapes for systolic blood pressure (P<.001), diastolic blood pressure (P=.001) and LDL cholesterol (P<.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Evaluating Association Shapes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figures 2 and 3
key_findings.note: The fitted curves print no values. Read approximately from the enlarged Figure 2 image (log scale): hypertension OR about 1.2 at 7, 2 at 14 and 4 to 5 at 21 drinks/week; coronary artery disease about 1.3, 2.8 and 9; the curves are fixed at OR 1 at zero intake. Figure 3 (approximate) shows systolic blood pressure about 12 mm Hg and LDL cholesterol about 35 mg/dL higher at 21 drinks/week.

key_findings.finding: With the secondary AUDIT-C-Restricted score, piecewise-linear analyses suggested a threshold: intake was not associated with higher cardiovascular risk until roughly 7 to 14 drinks/week, and slight decreases in risk with modest intake were seen for hypertension and in some analyses in women. The authors attribute these to residual pleiotropy in that score and to low power in sex-stratified analyses, because they were not seen with the ADH1B variant alone, after removing abstainers, or in other analyses. Multivariable nonlinear analysis adjusted for smoking, body mass index and depression supported the primary results.

Replication in 30 716 Mass General Brigham Biobank participants: the primary score was strongly associated with intake; nonlinear analysis again favoured a quadratic model for diastolic blood pressure (P<.001); the result for systolic blood pressure was not significant. No disease outcomes were analysed there.
key_findings.locator: Results › Nonlinear Genetic Associations in the Mass General Brigham Biobank

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge that the associations may reflect genes that influence both drinking and cardiovascular disease rather than an effect of alcohol itself, and that the primary score rests on variants for diagnosed alcohol use disorder, an indirect proxy for usual intake.

Correction notice (JAMA Netw Open 2022;5(4):e2212024, doi 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2022.12024): the first sentence of the abstract's Conclusions and Relevance should have said that adjustment for coincident, favourable lifestyle factors attenuated the observational benefits of modest intake. It changes wording only; all numbers on this card are unaffected.
key_findings.note: The PMC full text PMC8956974, read on 2026-10-27, still shows the uncorrected sentence in the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives women as 199 063 (53.49%); 199 063 of 371 463 is 53.59% (editors' arithmetic), and the men's and women's percentages as printed add to 99.90%.

The linear Mendelian randomization odds ratios are given per 1-SD difference in genetically predicted consumption (Abstract; Table 2 footnote), while the Methods say each instrument was standardized to a 1 drink/day increase and the allele-score results are per 1 drink/day; the SD is never defined.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Genetic Instruments for Alcohol Consumption; Table 2 footnote; Results › Traditional MR
reporting_issues.consequence: The linear estimates cannot be converted into grams or drinks; claims must keep the per-SD wording.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2's footnote says the disease associations were tested in current drinkers, but the text lists excluding abstainers as a secondary analysis, implying the primary analysis included them.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2 footnote; Results › Traditional MR, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which population the primary estimates come from; if restricted to current drinkers, the analysis conditions on a variable influenced by the genotype.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the secondary analyses and the analyses of other cardiovascular phenotypes supported the primary observations, but by the paper's own Bonferroni threshold (P<.008) myocardial infarction (P=2.00×10−2), stroke (P=2.10×10−2) and heart failure (P=9.00×10−3) were not significant.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Traditional MR, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims about myocardial infarction, stroke or heart failure from this paper should note that they did not meet its prespecified threshold.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Figure 3 says that the solid lines are odds ratio estimates, but the panels plot differences in γ-glutamyltransferase (U/L), LDL cholesterol (mg/dL) and blood pressure (mm Hg).
reporting_issues.consequence: Legend error; the plotted quantities are differences in the trait, not odds ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: Neither the observational hazard ratios (Figure 1) nor the fitted nonlinear curves (Figures 2 and 3) are given as numbers in the main text; the implied effect sizes at given intakes, which are very large on the plots, are not tabulated or discussed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of risk at a given intake cannot be cited from this paper except as approximate readings of plots; the statement that adjustment rendered moderate-intake associations non-significant cannot be checked numerically.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract on PMC still reads that coincident favourable lifestyle factors attenuated the observational benefits, although the correction of 20 April 2022 says the article has been corrected to attribute the attenuation to adjustment for those factors.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract (Conclusions and Relevance); correction notice PMC9021906
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims quoting the conclusion should use the corrected wording and cite the correction.
